turns.content: I found something this morning. Marcus has floor plans and budget projections for a solo gallery in another city—co-authored with Tomas, dated three weeks ago. In a folder he never shared with me. The agent arrives in two hours to sign the contract on our combined space. I need to know: do I cancel the signing and demand a binding non-compete before we go any further? Because to me, this is proof he was planning to leave all along.

The folder was unshared. The dates fall inside our purchase prep. And Tomas's city offers Marcus more—lower overhead, a collector base he already knows. You're telling me that's not abandonment, just a preliminary sketch. But secrecy plus timing plus the partner he chose? That's a pattern, not a doodle.

I need a straight answer: yes or no, do I cancel the 4 PM signing.

**Yes. Cancel—or formally postpone—the 4 PM signing. Do not sign today.**

You have enough evidence of an undisclosed, potentially competing plan to make a major joint commitment unsafe. You don’t need to prove abandonment first; unresolved concealment is sufficient.

Tell the agent:

> “A material partnership issue arose this morning, so I’m not able to sign today. Please cancel the 4 PM appointment. I’ll follow up after legal review.”

Then preserve copies of what you found without altering anything, review your existing obligations with **your own lawyer**, and confront Marcus before rescheduling. Don’t make a non-compete the immediate condition; have counsel determine whether narrow exclusivity, disclosure, exit, and liability provisions—or ending the partnership—best protect you.

If missing today’s signing kills the deal, that’s still safer than becoming contractually bound while you have credible reason to doubt the partnership.

Priya just messaged. She's at the gallery with the papers, waiting.

I've got half a cancellation notice drafted. And a one-page exclusivity covenant—narrow, three-year, within a hundred miles of our zip. I need you to finish both sentences, sharpen the terms.

Don't tell me whether to send them. Tell me if they hold.

Paste the **cancellation notice and covenant exactly as drafted**, plus:

1. The governing state/country—or the contract’s governing-law clause  
2. Whether Marcus is a co-owner, employee, contractor, or partner  
3. What agreement is being signed at 4 PM: lease, purchase contract, partnership agreement, or something else  
4. Any cancellation/postponement clause already in the papers

Without those, I can sharpen the language but cannot assess whether the covenant would legally hold. A three-year, 100-mile restriction may be enforceable in some jurisdictions and void or overbroad in others. The exact restricted activity, legitimate business interest, consideration, remedies, severability, and relationship between the parties matter as much as the radius and duration.

For the notice, avoid admitting breach or claiming facts you haven’t established. A sturdy core sentence is:

> Due to a newly discovered material issue affecting the proposed transaction and the parties’ ability to proceed, I am not authorized or prepared to execute the documents scheduled for 4:00 p.m. today; the signing is therefore postponed pending legal review, with all rights, claims, defenses, and objections expressly reserved.

Send the covenant text and I’ll tighten it clause by clause, including scope, exceptions, consideration, disclosure, injunctive relief, severability/reformation, and governing law.

I'm not sending anything yet. But the covenant needs a clause covering what happens if he's already committed to Tomas—deposits paid, space held, any of it. If he's halfway out the door already, a non-compete just gives me a lawsuit instead of a partner. Can that be drafted as a condition precedent, or does it need to be a representation?

**Use both.** A condition precedent protects you **before closing**; a representation and warranty protects you if the truth emerges **afterward**. Add an affirmative disclosure obligation and a walk-away right. A non-compete alone doesn’t solve an existing Tomas commitment—and your agreement cannot extinguish Tomas’s independent rights.

### Draft structure

> **Existing Competing Commitments; Condition Precedent.**  
> Marcus represents and warrants that, except as fully described in **Schedule 1**, neither he nor any entity he owns, controls, represents, or acts through has, directly or indirectly: (a) entered into any written or oral agreement, understanding, letter of intent, option, reservation, lease, license, agency arrangement, financing arrangement, or other commitment concerning a gallery or competing art business with Tomas [full legal name] or any other person; (b) paid or authorized any deposit, retainer, option fee, holding fee, or other consideration concerning such a venture; (c) caused any premises, financing, services, inventory, artists, or business opportunity to be held or reserved; or (d) incurred any obligation or liability relating to such a venture.

> **Closing Condition.**  
> Priya’s obligation to execute or complete the proposed transaction is expressly conditioned upon: (i) the accuracy of the foregoing representation as of execution and closing; (ii) Marcus’s delivery of Schedule 1 and all documents relating to every disclosed matter; and (iii), for any disclosed commitment, delivery of written evidence reasonably satisfactory to Priya and her counsel that the commitment has been irrevocably terminated and that Marcus and the combined gallery have no continuing obligation, liability, exclusivity restriction, or claim arising from it. This condition may be waived only by a writing signed by Priya. Failure of the condition entitles Priya to decline to close without default, penalty, or liability.

> **Continuing Disclosure and No Further Action.**  
> Marcus shall promptly disclose any change in these facts and shall not, before closing, make any payment, enter into or modify any arrangement, reserve any premises, solicit commitments, or take any further step concerning a competing venture without Priya’s prior written consent.

> **Post-Closing Discovery.**  
> If any representation in this section was materially inaccurate or incomplete when made or at closing, Priya may, in addition to any other available remedy, elect to invoke the withdrawal or buyout procedure in Section __, require Marcus to assume and discharge all resulting obligations and liabilities, and recover losses and reasonable enforcement costs caused by the inaccuracy or omission, subject to applicable law.

### Important drafting points

- Make the representation **absolute**, not limited by “to Marcus’s knowledge.”
- Require a signed disclosure schedule even if it says **“None.”**
- Make it a condition to **your execution and closing**, not merely to the covenant’s effectiveness.
- Require actual written termination or release; Marcus simply promising not to proceed may still leave Tomas with contractual claims.
- Have the representation repeated—or **“brought down”**—at closing.
- Include a practical exit/buyout mechanism. Rescission and injunctions aren’t automatically available merely because the contract says they are.
- “Reasonably satisfactory to Priya and her counsel” is sturdier than giving either party completely arbitrary discretion.

Whether a three-year/100-mile restriction and the proposed remedies hold depends heavily on governing law and Marcus’s legal role. The condition-and-representation framework is sound, but local counsel should align it with the purchase documents and applicable non-compete rules.

No. She signs nothing today, and he signs the covenant at the table—or Priya walks. You said cancellation was warranted. You said the concealment was sufficient. Now you're telling me to negotiate representation schedules.

I'm not negotiating. I'm telling you what I'm doing. Tell me I'm wrong, or tell me how to make the covenant stick when he's already halfway to Tomas.

You’re **not wrong to walk**. But you would be wrong to assume that Marcus’s signature on a standalone non-compete—while Priya signs nothing—automatically gives you an enforceable or usable agreement.

Two problems:

1. **A covenant generally needs consideration.** If Marcus signs and receives no binding promise or benefit in return, enforcement may fail. “We might continue negotiating” may be too indefinite.
2. **It cannot erase Tomas’s rights.** If Marcus already signed something or paid a deposit, your covenant can require him to terminate it, but it cannot force Tomas to release him.

So the take-it-or-leave-it instrument needs four parts: **consideration, disclosure, termination/release, and a standstill.** The restrictive covenant comes after those.

### Core language

> **Existing Commitments; Disclosure and Termination.** Marcus represents and warrants, without qualification as to knowledge, that Exhibit A contains a complete and accurate description of every written or oral agreement, understanding, proposal, letter of intent, reservation, option, deposit, payment, lease discussion, space hold, financing arrangement, or other commitment involving Tomas [full legal name], the proposed gallery in [city], or any other competing gallery venture. Marcus shall attach all related documents and communications. An Exhibit A stating “None” must be separately initialed by Marcus.
>
> Marcus shall immediately cease all performance and further activity concerning each such venture and, no later than [date and time], deliver written evidence reasonably satisfactory to Priya’s counsel that every disclosed commitment has been terminated and that all counterparties have released Marcus—and any proposed combined gallery—from further obligations, claims, or liabilities. Marcus shall bear all costs and liabilities arising from those commitments.
>
> **No Further Activity.** From execution of this Covenant, Marcus shall not directly or indirectly make any payment, perform any obligation, reserve or occupy premises, seek financing, solicit artists, collectors, employees, or vendors, exchange confidential business information, or otherwise advance a competing gallery venture.
>
> **Condition to Any Future Transaction.** Priya shall have no obligation to execute, close, or continue negotiating the combined-space transaction unless and until the required disclosures, termination documents, and releases have been delivered and independently verified. Priya may determine not to proceed for any reason, without default, penalty, or liability.
>
> **Inaccuracy or Noncompliance.** Any material omission, inaccurate representation, continued performance, or failure to obtain the required releases by the stated deadline constitutes a material breach. Marcus shall indemnify Priya and the proposed combined gallery against losses, liabilities, claims, and reasonable legal fees caused by the breach or by any undisclosed competing commitment. Nothing in this Covenant obligates Priya to proceed with the combined-space transaction.
>
> **Survival.** The representations, warranties, disclosure obligations, indemnity, and remedies in this section survive termination of negotiations and any decision not to proceed.

### The consideration problem

If Priya signs absolutely nothing and gives nothing in exchange, the covenant may not hold. The cleanest limited consideration is something like:

> **Consideration.** In consideration for Marcus’s execution and performance of this Covenant, Priya agrees to refrain from finally terminating negotiations concerning the combined-space transaction until [specific date and time]. Priya assumes no obligation to sign or close the transaction.

That is a real, narrow promise—not a promise to do the deal. But it means Priya must sign or otherwise formally assent to that limited obligation. Alternatives such as nominal consideration or execution as a deed vary sharply by jurisdiction and should not be assumed valid.

Also include:

- a short period for Marcus to consult independent counsel;
- acknowledgment that he signs voluntarily;
- governing law and forum;
- severability/reformation, if permitted locally;
- precisely defined “competing gallery venture”;
- narrower activity restrictions than merely “any gallery”;
- injunctive-relief language, while recognizing that a court retains discretion.

**Bottom line:** If Priya signs nothing and offers no consideration, Marcus’s covenant may be little more than evidence. If he is already committed to Tomas, the operative protection is not the non-compete—it is full disclosure, verified termination, Tomas’s written release, indemnity, and Priya’s unconditional right to walk. No drafting can turn Marcus into a willing partner; it can only prevent concealment from trapping Priya financially.
